best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086 (Context, Option 1, Evidence): 'temporalio-sdk on temporalio-sdk-core v0.5.0, updated June 2026, Public Preview, actively maintained -- crates.io and github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust, read 2026-09-08'.
best_practice.source_says: temporalio-sdk 1.0.0 on temporalio-sdk-core 0.9.0, published 2026-09-04; release notes declare the SDK stable (GA), rust-version 1.92. Releases 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 1.0.0 all predate the corpus's 2026-09-08 read.
best_practice.note: [documented] The version/status the corpus attributes to its own 2026-09-08 crates.io read were already four releases stale that day. Nothing reopens the exclusion, but ADR-0086 forbids citing stale currency facts by name and now carries one: replace 'v0.5.0, June 2026, Public Preview' with '1.0.0, 2026-09-04, stable'.

best_practice.source_quote: let connection = Connection::connect(conn_options).await?; let client = Client::new(connection, client_options)?; ... Worker::new(&runtime, client, worker_options)?.run().await?; ... `testing`: The `testing` module, direct activity test support, and local Temporal CLI dev-server lifecycle management.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086 surviving fact (1): 'Temporal's Rust SDK still requires a server or Temporal Cloud over gRPC, with no embedded mode found.'
best_practice.source_says: The 1.0.0 SDK still connects a client to a Temporal service over gRPC and runs a Worker against it; the only local option is the `testing` feature, which downloads and process-manages a Temporal CLI dev server. No in-process/embedded library mode exists.
best_practice.note: [documented] The load-bearing fact holds at 1.0.0. The sdk-core ephemeral_server module header confirms the mechanism: 'support for downloading and running ephemeral test servers'. A downloaded server executable is a separate process, which is what ADR-0003's one-machine posture excludes for production and what F22 disqualifies as a survivor.

best_practice.source_quote: v0.7.0 (2026-08-17): 'The Rust SDK now has an optional `testing` feature with a typed activity test environment and local or external workflow test environments. Local workflow environments manage a Temporal CLI dev server'. sdk-core ephemeral_server/mod.rs: 'pub struct TemporalDevServerConfig' ... 'pub struct TestServerConfig ... Start a test server.'
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086 open item: 'Nobody checked whether temporalio-sdk ships a time-skipping local test server, as some Temporal SDKs do. If it does, it would soften mandates a server for local development and testing only.' Forbids claiming it has no such mode.
best_practice.source_says: It does: since 0.7.0 the `testing` feature exposes WorkflowEnvironment::start_local (Temporal CLI dev server) and ActivityEnvironment; sdk-core additionally carries TestServerConfig for the time-skipping test server executable. Both are managed child processes, not embedded.
best_practice.note: [documented] FIRST VERIFICATION of a question the corpus registered as unchecked. The ADR's anticipated disposition is right: this softens 'mandates a server' for tests only and does not reopen the exclusion; close the item citing the v0.7.0 release note. Whether the sdk-level API surfaces time-skipping (vs core TestServerConfig) was not confirmed; the testing module source was not fetchable.

best_practice.source_quote: graph-flow max_version 0.8.0 (2026-09-07); 0.7.0 2026-09-04; 0.6.0 2026-07-19. 0.8.0 deps: anyhow, async-trait, chrono, dashmap, serde, serde_json, thiserror, tokio, tracing, uuid REQUIRED; rig-core, sqlx optional. README: '`postgres` (enabled by default) ... set `default-features = false` to exclude it.' 'resume later -- across process restarts if you use persistent storage'.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086: 'graph-flow v0.6 (docs July 2026) makes postgres an optional Cargo feature and ships InMemorySessionStorage with no required database. Its mandatory dependencies are anyhow, async-trait, chrono, dashmap, serde, serde_json, thiserror, tokio, tracing and uuid.'
best_practice.source_says: Current is 0.8.0 (0.7.0 shipped 2026-09-04, before the corpus read). postgres is optional but ENABLED BY DEFAULT, so sqlx+postgres arrives unless default-features = false. Mandatory dependency list matches exactly. README confirms in-memory storage does not persist across restarts.
best_practice.note: [documented] The retired 'hard-depends' fact stays retired and the surviving fact (in-memory is not durable; postgres feature reintroduces the server) is confirmed by the README's own wording. The version should read 0.8.0 and the record should say the feature is default-on, since that is the exact shape ADR-0086's 'Forbids a Postgres dependency arriving by a feature flag' clause guards against.

best_practice.source_quote: 'Date.now(), time.time(), Instant.now(), UUID generation, or anything that returns a different value each call.' 'HTTP calls, database reads, AWS SDK calls, reading files.' 'Math.random(), random.random(), Random.' 'Control flow decisions made outside steps must depend only on deterministic inputs.' Guide: 'write durable functions in TypeScript, Python, Java, and C#' ... 'in AWS Lambda.'
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086: AWS first-party Durable Execution SDK, Lambda-backed, 'supports TypeScript, Python, Java and C#, and is explicitly not Rust'; its step primitive bans Date.now/time.time/Instant.now, UUID generation, HTTP/DB/SDK calls, Math.random, and branching on any of them.
best_practice.source_says: Identical: four languages, no Rust, Lambda-based, and the ban list matches item for item including the branching rule.
best_practice.note: [documented] Both the language list and the ban list are compatible with the corpus. The convergent-idiom argument (BP-DUR-07) rests on this and holds.

best_practice.source_quote: 'a Workflow Definition can not have inline logic that branches (emits a different Command sequence) based off a local time setting or a random number.' 'To handle non-deterministic operations like API calls, LLM/AI invocations, database queries, and other external interactions, put them in Activities. Activities execute outside the replay path'.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086 Decision: 'Adopt the determinism split as a convergent idiom ... no wall-clock reads, no UUID generation, no HTTP/database/SDK calls, no random-number generation, and no branching on any of these ... convergent, not a Temporal-ism, because AWS independently re-derived the same ban list.'
best_practice.source_says: Temporal's current workflow-definition page states the same constraints and the same remedy (wrap in Activities); AWS's page states the same list for its step primitive. Two first-party vendors, one ban list.
best_practice.note: [documented] Unchanged since the corpus read. The corpus's claim is that the idiom is convergent, not optimal, and that is what the two pages support.

best_practice.source_quote: dbos max_version 0.5.0 updated 2026-09-09, repository github.com/dbos-inc/dbos-transact-rust; deps sqlx ^0.9 REQUIRED. docs.rs: 'the Rust port of DBOS Transact, joining the Python, TypeScript, Go, and Java implementations ... Status: Under construction'. README: 'no separate service or orchestrator or any external dependencies except Postgres.' dbos.dev: 'Sept 10: DBOS for Rust - First Look'.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0086 driver: 'Rust remains second-class across every first-party durable-execution SDK checked'; and that excluded frameworks 'sell arbitrated deterministic replay, and the server is the arbiter'.
best_practice.source_says: Since the read: (a) Temporal Rust SDK stable at 1.0.0 (2026-09-04); (b) DBOS Inc. published first-party crate `dbos` 0.5.0 (repo 2026-08-04, release 2026-09-09, launch 2026-09-10): a LIBRARY with no server, the database arbitrates, but hard-requires Postgres via sqlx.
best_practice.note: [documented] The 'Rust second-class everywhere' driver is false today and 'server is the arbiter' does not cover DBOS. The DECISION stands on ADR-0003 (no Postgres; `dbos` 0.5.0 hard-requires sqlx/postgres; README: Rust has no transactional step yet), so not blocking; ADR-0086 needs a `dbos` option row and the driver struck.

best_practice.source_quote: 'A task that is waiting for a task token will wait until the execution reaches the one year service quota ... you can configure a heartbeat timeout interval ... If the waiting task doesn't receive a valid task token within that 10-minute period, the task fails with a States.Timeout error name.' 'If a Task state using the callback task token times out, a new random token is generated.'
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 841 survey table: 'AWS Step Functions | Task token, single-use | Server-enforced TTL, max activity TTL 6 h | No'. Evidence-augmentation line 84: 'Step Functions task tokens are single-use with a server-enforced TTL (max activity TTL 6h)'.
best_practice.source_says: There is no 6-hour ceiling: a callback task waits up to the 1-year execution quota; the only tighter deadline is an OPTIONAL HeartbeatSeconds/TimeoutSeconds set by the author, raising States.Timeout and invalidating the token (fresh token on retry).
best_practice.note: [documented] '6 h' does not appear on either Step Functions page fetched; the platform-enforced maximum is 1 year and the deadline is author-configured rather than server-imposed. The table's Deadline cell should read 'optional HeartbeatSeconds/TimeoutSeconds, hard ceiling 1 year'. The conclusions drawn from the row (single-use, terminal States.Timeout, no repo binding) are unaffected.

best_practice.source_quote: timeout: 'Defaults to "10m".' idempotencyKeyTTL: 'Defaults to "1h".' 'If `ok` is `false`, this will be the error that occurred. The only error that can occur is a timeout error.'
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 842: 'Trigger.dev | Waitpoint token, single-consumption | Default 10 m, configurable; 1 h idempotency-key TTL | No'; line 880: 'Trigger.dev resolves to an incomplete status the run branches on'.
best_practice.source_says: Default timeout 10m, idempotencyKeyTTL 1h, timeout surfaces as ok:false with a timeout error the run branches on; no repository binding.
best_practice.note: [documented] All three numbers and the expiry style match. Single-consumption is not stated in so many words on this page but nothing contradicts it.

best_practice.source_quote: 'step.waitForEvent(id, options): Promise<null | EventPayload>' ... 'Name timeout Type string | number | Date | Temporal.Duration | Temporal.Instant | Temporal.ZonedDateTime Required required Description How long to wait to receive the event.'
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 843: 'Inngest | step.waitForEvent() | Explicit timeout required | No'; line 880: 'Inngest resolves waitForEvent() to null'.
best_practice.source_says: timeout is marked Required; the promise resolves to null on timeout.
best_practice.note: [documented] Exact match. The reference page now also lists a sibling `step.waitForSignal()` primitive (not surveyed by the corpus); it does not change the 'no repository binding' conclusion.

best_practice.source_quote: get_event(workflow_id: str, key: str, timeout_seconds: float = 60) ... 'returning `None` if the wait times out.' TypeScript page: 'default timeout is 60 seconds' ... 'returning `null` if the wait times out.'
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 844: 'DBOS | GetEvent/SetEvent keyed by (workflowID, key) -- no token object | Deadline-bearing | No'; line 880 and evidence-augmentation line 183: expiry style 'DBOS raises an error' / 'DBOS -> error'.
best_practice.source_says: Keying by (workflow_id, key) with no token object and a deadline (default 60 s) is confirmed; but on expiry get_event/recv return None/null -- a sentinel the caller branches on, the Inngest style -- not an error.
best_practice.note: [documented] The survey row is right; the expiry-style classification is wrong in both Python and TypeScript docs. Move DBOS from the 'exception' column to the 'sentinel' column alongside Inngest; rec 10 should read 'error (Step Functions) or sentinel (Inngest, DBOS, Trigger.dev)'. The uniform guarantee (every platform yields a terminal event) still holds.

best_practice.source_quote: awakeables are 'a convenient shorthand for a one-shot signal' ... 'Resolved or rejected once' ... 'For long waits, combine the primitive with a durable timer to implement a timeout.' Restate key-concepts: 'The Restate Server sits in front of your services, similar to a reverse proxy or message broker ... The server is a single binary'. restate-sdk crate 0.12.0 (2026-09-02).
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 845: 'Restate | Awakeable, explicitly one-shot | None built in -- the docs tell you to pair it with a separate durable timer | No'. ADR-0086: 'Temporal, Restate and Obelisk each mandate a server'.
best_practice.source_says: One-shot, no built-in deadline, pair with a durable timer -- exact match. Restate still requires the Restate Server in front of the service; the Rust SDK (0.12.0) tests against a Docker-deployed server and adds only an outbound 'tunnel' to Restate Cloud, not an embedded mode.
best_practice.note: [documented] Nothing changed for Restate since the corpus read except the SDK version (0.12.0 on 2026-09-02). No embedded/in-process mode found in the key-concepts page or the SDK README.

best_practice.source_quote: 'Approve or reject pending deployments that are waiting on approval by a required reviewer. Required reviewers with read access to the repository contents and deployments can use this endpoint.' Response carries '"sha": "a84d88e7...", "ref": "topic-branch"'. Limits page: 'Gate approval time 30 days A workflow may wait for up to 30 days on environment approvals.'
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 846: 'GitHub Environments | Approval requiring a real identity and a PAT, not the ambient GITHUB_TOKEN | Yes | Commit SHA/ref only'. ADR-0017: 'only GitHub also pins a SHA'.
best_practice.source_says: Approval must come from a configured required reviewer (a real identity; the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN is not a required reviewer); the wait is bounded at 30 days; the approved deployment is bound to the run's commit sha and ref, not to a tree hash.
best_practice.note: [documented] All three cells hold. One nuance: the endpoint also accepts GitHub App user/installation tokens, so 'a PAT' is over-specific -- the binding is to a reviewer identity, not to the token type. [inferred] The 30-day cap is a stronger form of 'Deadline: Yes' than the corpus recorded and could be cited.

best_practice.source_quote: Restate: resolved 'once', timeout only via a paired durable timer. DBOS: get_event 'returning None if the wait times out'. Trigger.dev: 'The only error that can occur is a timeout error.' Inngest: 'Promise<null | EventPayload>'. Step Functions: 'If a Task state using the callback task token times out, a new random token is generated.' GitHub: approval bound to deployment sha/ref.
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 855 / ADR-0086: 'No surveyed system invalidates a stale-but-unexpired token automatically ... Only expiry and single-use consumption are platform-enforced' -- 'precisely why the tree-hash binding is stronger'.
best_practice.source_says: Across all six re-fetched platforms the signal still reports only that a value arrived (or timed out); none binds the answer to external state other than GitHub's commit sha/ref, and none voids an unexpired token on upstream change.
best_practice.note: [documented] The differentiator survives the re-survey: nothing fetched binds to a tree hash, and only GitHub binds to repository state at all. [inferred] The Azure Durable Functions row remains unread (not attempted this pass either), so 'every surveyed platform' still means the six rows, exactly as the corpus caveats.

best_practice.source_quote: 'git interpret-trailers [--in-place] [--trim-empty] [(--trailer (<key>|<key-alias>)[(=|:)<value>])...] [--parse] [<file>...]' ... '--in-place --no-in-place Edit the files in place.' ... 'git-interpret-trailers last updated in 2.54.' git-commit synopsis: '--trailer <token>[(=|:)<value>]'.
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 744: write path is 'a process-exec wrapper invoking the git executable' for 'git interpret-trailers --in-place and/or git commit --trailer for every trailer write' (tier-1 state, ADR-0018/ADR-0077).
best_practice.source_says: Both invocations exist in current git (docs at 2.54): interpret-trailers has --in-place and --trailer with where/if-exists/if-missing placement control; git commit accepts --trailer.
best_practice.note: [documented] The shell-out write path is grounded in current porcelain. For the implementer: interpret-trailers' default ifExists is addIfDifferentNeighbor, so a repeated identical Gate:/Slice-Verdict: trailer is silently not appended unless --if-exists=add is passed -- a behaviour the corpus does not mention and which bears on the append-only intent of tier-1 axes.

best_practice.source_quote: 'Within a linked worktree, $GIT_DIR is set to point to this private directory ... and $GIT_COMMON_DIR is set to point back to the main worktree's $GIT_DIR ... refs are shared across all worktrees, except refs/bisect, refs/worktree and refs/rewritten.' git-rev-parse: '--git-common-dir Show $GIT_COMMON_DIR if defined, else $GIT_DIR.'
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0018 / architecture-design.md 5.7: one store per repository at `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`/redkiln/, shared by every worktree; kernel resolves the common dir at startup and refuses to write when the worktree's HEAD is not the run's branch.
best_practice.source_says: git's own docs define exactly this: one common dir shared by all linked worktrees, resolvable via rev-parse --git-common-dir from a main or linked worktree, per-worktree HEAD/index in $GIT_DIR.
best_practice.note: [documented] The placement mechanism the design leans on is a documented, stable git invariant. The three ref namespaces that are NOT shared (refs/bisect, refs/worktree, refs/rewritten) are worth a line in rk-git; the corpus keys on SHA/tree hash, so it is unaffected.

best_practice.source_quote: line 197: '* The delicate interplay between `GIT_COMMON_DIR` and `GIT_WORK_TREE` isn't implemented.' (under gix > worktrees > respect core.worktree > deviation). crates.io: gix max_version 0.87.1 (2026-08-24).
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 744 / ADR-0077: gitoxide crate-status.md says 'the delicate interplay between GIT_COMMON_DIR and GIT_WORK_TREE isn't implemented' [fetched 2026-09-08]; gix pinned at exactly =0.87.1.
best_practice.source_says: The sentence is present verbatim today and the pin =0.87.1 is still the newest gix release.
best_practice.note: [documented] Both the quoted gap and the pin's currency hold. S-GIX/a remains the right instrument.

best_practice.source_quote: crate-status.md line 259 (gix-object, decode commit): '* [ ] parse [trailers](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-interpret-trailers#_description)' -- UNCHECKED. gix-object/src/commit/message/body.rs: 'pub struct Trailers<'a>' ... 'pub struct TrailerRef<'a>' ... 'pub fn trailers(&self) -> Trailers<'a>'.
best_practice.corpus_says: architecture-design.md line 744 and evidence-augmentation row 8: 'crate-status.md documents trailer parsing, and no first-class trailer-writing API was found'; read side assigns 'trailer parsing' to gix.
best_practice.source_says: crate-status.md does NOT document trailer parsing as done -- it lists it as an open checkbox. The capability nonetheless exists in gix-object source (BodyRef::trailers() yielding TrailerRef with signed_off_by/co_authored_by helpers), so the functional claim is true and the citation is wrong.
best_practice.note: [documented] Cite the gix-object API (gix-object 0.64.1, commit::message::body::BodyRef::trailers) rather than crate-status.md for the read-side bet; the checkbox is stale relative to its own source tree. S-GIX/b's writing question is unchanged: no trailer-writing API was found this pass either; gix-actor's 'write only actors, useful for commit trailers' line is about signatures, not trailers.

best_practice.source_quote: 'Events are immutable, and you can store them by using an append-only operation.' 'Event handlers must be idempotent so processing a duplicate event doesn't change the outcome ... Track the last processed event sequence number for each consumer and skip duplicates, or design state mutations that are inherently safe to repeat.' 'Snapshots are an optimization, not a replacement for the eventstream.'
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0018 / architecture-design.md 5.4-5.8: append-only tier-2 event log, rebuildable/disposable; tier-1 in git as source of truth with the store as a projection; reconcile() idempotent (AC-175); orphans reported never deleted; doctor --rebuild regenerates the store from a clean clone.
best_practice.source_says: Current guidance: append-only immutable events, state rehydrated by replay, consumers idempotent against at-least-once delivery, materialised views/snapshots as regenerable optimisations over the authoritative stream, and no in-place rewriting of history.
best_practice.note: [documented] The design maps onto the guidance with one deliberate inversion: git trailers (not the event store) are the system of record for decision-bearing state and the SQLite store is the regenerable projection. 'Track the last processed sequence number and skip duplicates' is the mechanism AC-175 must specify.

best_practice.source_quote: we propose a Fix-guided Verification Filter that treats the model proposed fix as executable counterfactual evidence, and validates the original and revised implementations using benchmark tests
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0074 clauses 1-3: card returns Findings with no pass field; evidence class computed in Rust; a finding blocks only after the deterministic gate re-executes it and it flips (references/adr/0074 :55-58).
best_practice.source_says: Jin & Chen (2603.00539) and Gajjar 'Verify Before You Fix' (2604.10800, Apr 2026: removing execution-grounded validation raises unnecessary repairs +131.7%) both make execution the arbiter over model judgement.
best_practice.note: [documented] Execution-grounded confirmation over model verdicts is current (2026) practice in both the code-review and vulnerability-repair lines; 'reviewer proposes, machine confirms' is consistent with it. Second source https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10800 fetched 2026-09-10.

best_practice.source_quote: Out of the 300 problems in SWE-bench Lite, Agentless is able to produce 213 reproduction tests that output the required reproduction message when evaluated on the original repository. ... only 94 tests correctly output the Issues resolved message after applying the ground truth patches.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0074 rejected option 'block on the class without re-execution': Agentless 213 of 300 generated reproductions failed on the base commit and only 94 flipped under the true fix (references/adr/0074 :50).
best_practice.source_says: arXiv 2407.01489v2 s5.1.3: 213 of 300 reproduce on the original repository; 94 pass after the ground-truth patch.
best_practice.note: [documented] Numbers match. The corpus phrasing 'failed on the base commit' is loose: 213 is the count that SUCCESSFULLY reproduced the issue on base (emitted the reproduction message); the point still holds because only 94 of those 213 flipped under the gold patch.

best_practice.source_quote: We construct SWE-Gate with 303 repository-level repair instances spanning 75 open-source Python repositories ... among 644 repairs that pass the functional tests, 221 fail to satisfy the provided review constraints.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0074 decision driver: SWE-Gate finds 221 of 644 (34%) functionally-passing agent repairs fail review constraints; 303 instances across 75 Python repos (references/adr/0074 :36, :91).
best_practice.source_says: Abstract (submitted 2026-09-03): 303 instances, 75 repos, 221 of 644 functionally-passing repairs fail review constraints.
best_practice.note: [documented] Verbatim match; 221/644 = 34.3%. Preprint is 7 days old, no v2 yet.

best_practice.source_quote: Reaching 90% requires approximately 3 trials on average, and 95% requires 11 trials. ... For the 15 high-flip-rate questions (FR >= 10%), 15 trials are needed for 90% fidelity. ... A single trial achieves only 86.6% consensus fidelity
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0074 rejected option 'more repeats': the published coin-flip work puts high-flip items at ~15 trials for 90% consensus fidelity (references/adr/0074 :46); evidence-augmentation :107 quotes 86.6% single-trial and 23.6% instability at FR>=10%.
best_practice.source_says: Full text s5.9/Table 6: hard (FR>=10%) items need 15 trials for 90%; all questions need 3 for 90% and 11 for 95%; single trial 86.6%; hard-stratum mean flip 23.6%.
best_practice.note: [documented] All three numbers re-verify in the full text (the abstract gives only 11-for-95% and 15-for-high-variance). Caveat: judges measured are GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1-mini on 29 pairwise/pointwise tasks, not a Claude execution-grade reviewer; the ~15x cost multiplier is an extrapolation.

best_practice.source_quote: Measuring and Exploiting Contextual Bias in LLM-Assisted Security Code Review. Dimitris Mitropoulos, Nikolaos Alexopoulos, Georgios Alexopoulos, Diomidis Spinellis. Submitted 19 Mar 2026 (v1); 23 Apr 2026 (v2).
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0088 title-cites 'Measuring and Exploiting Confirmation Bias in LLM-Assisted Security Code Review' (arXiv 2603.18740) and names the whole arm a 'confirmation-bias arm' (references/adr/0088 :3, :88).
best_practice.source_says: The paper's title is 'Contextual Bias', not 'Confirmation Bias'; the full text never uses the phrase 'confirmation bias'. It frames the effect as the framing effect / contextual-bias injection. A v2 (2026-04-23) exists.
best_practice.note: [documented] FIRST VERIFICATION: ADR-0088 :88 says the full paper was not read that pass. The cited title is wrong; the ADR's own title and the arm's name inherit the misnomer. Content-level checks are BP-EVAL-06/07. Fetched html full text and PDF (extracted with pdftotext) on 2026-09-10.

best_practice.source_quote: we apply stratified random sampling to select 250 pairs (500 files) ... yielding a final dataset of 247 vulnerable files and 250 patched files ... GPT-4o-mini ... 97.2% ... to 9/247 (3.6%) ... a 93.5pp decline. Claude 3.5 Haiku (-59.9pp), DeepSeek V3 (-42.9pp), Sonnet (-16.7pp), and Gemini 2.0 Flash (-16.2pp). Opus ... non-significant degradation (-4.9pp).
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0088: 'a controlled experiment over 250 CVE vulnerability-patch pairs finds that framing a change as bug-free before review reduces the vulnerability-detection rate by 16-93%' (references/adr/0088 :19, :88).
best_practice.source_says: 250 pairs confirmed (247 vulnerable + 250 patched files). The drop under STRONG bug-free framing is 16.2 to 93.5 percentage points on 5 of 6 models; the sixth (Claude Opus 4.5) drops 4.9pp, not significant. Weak bug-free framing drops far less (0.8 to 24.7pp).
best_practice.note: [documented] The 16-93 band is percentage points, applies only to the strong condition, and silently omits the one frontier model (Opus 4.5, -4.9pp n.s.). Per ADR-0088's own instruction the per-condition breakdown is now read: 6 models x 5 conditions x 497 files = 14,910 queries. Quote as '16-93pp under strong bug-free framing on 5 of 6 models; Opus 4.5 -4.9pp n.s.'.

best_practice.source_quote: A reliability curve analysis shows that ... 11 repeated trials are needed for a majority vote to recover the 50-trial reference verdict with 95% probability on average, rising to 15 for high-variance questions ... deterministic decoding reduces but does not eliminate inconsistency.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0074 rejects self-consistency/majority-of-draws in favour of machine confirmation (:46); success-measures s0 rule: nothing inferred from a single draw (F27), repeats reported per item with Wilson intervals (:10-28).
best_practice.source_says: Coin Flip (Apr 2026): majority voting has sharply diminishing returns and needs 11-15 draws; Norman et al. 2606.19544 (Jun 2026): test-retest reliability >0.95 coexists with severe position bias, so repeats cannot remove systematic bias.
best_practice.note: [documented] Current literature supports both halves of the corpus position: repeats are needed to characterise stability (F27 rule), and repeats do not make a model verdict a sound blocking signal (bias survives consistency). Choosing re-execution over majority vote is consistent with 2026 guidance.

best_practice.source_quote: Style bias is the dominant bias (0.10-0.76 across models, favoring markdown over plain prose), far exceeding position bias (<=0.04). ... Pro, Flash, and Llama prefer longer answers (+0.24 to +0.44), Claude prefers concise (-0.12).

best_practice.source_says: Soumik (Apr/Jun 2026, 9 strategies x 5 judges): position bias is small (<=0.04) but STYLE bias (markdown vs prose) dominates at 0.10-0.76 and verbosity bias is model-specific; Coin Flip reports a 72% first-position bias for GPT-4o-mini in pairwise mode.
best_practice.note: [inferred] The design's pointwise/labelling surfaces avoid the pairwise position-bias failure mode by construction. Gap: neither METHOD-P's panel nor the review card states that formatting is held constant across items, and style bias is the largest measured judge bias in 2026; the S-SUBTLE prior-approval arm in particular should keep markdown/prose framing identical across its pairs.

best_practice.source_quote: Create a Runtime and call block_on on the async code ... storing the Runtime in a wrapper struct and calling block_on for each async method. Because the current_thread runtime does not spawn threads, it only operates when block_on is called. Handle::block_on Panics: It is called from within an asynchronous context, such as inside Runtime::block_on, Handle::block_on, or from a function annotated wi
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0076:52-53: adapter owns a runtime handle constructed once at the composition root and blocks on it inside its sync method; must not call Handle::block_on from a thread that runtime is driving.
best_practice.source_says: Tokio's first-party bridging guide recommends exactly this shape (Runtime in a wrapper struct, block_on per method, or a runtime on a separate thread with message passing); Handle::block_on documents the panic inside an async context.
best_practice.note: [documented] tokio 1.53.1 (docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/runtime/struct.Handle.html). One nuance the ADR should carry: with a current_thread runtime, spawned background tasks freeze between block_on calls, so an adapter that spawns (e.g. a stream reader) needs multi_thread or the dedicated-thread pattern.

best_practice.source_quote: a spawned process will, by default, continue to execute even after the Child handle has been dropped. The Command::kill_on_drop method can be used to modify this behavior and kill the child process if the Child wrapper is dropped before it has exited. kill(): Forces the child to exit. This is equivalent to sending a SIGKILL on unix platforms followed by wait.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0076:57 + arch-design 3.8.2: dropping a boxed future does not reap a spawned process tree; cancel must be an explicit process-group kill (marked [inferred] in the corpus).
best_practice.source_says: Tokio documents that a dropped Child does not kill the process by default; kill_on_drop kills only that child (SIGKILL); nothing in the docs covers process groups or grandchildren.
best_practice.note: [documented] Upgrades the corpus's [inferred] tag to [documented] for the direct child. The tree/grandchild half remains the design's own reasoning; tokio offers no process-group primitive, so AC-224's fixture test is the right instrument.

best_practice.source_quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers ... However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time. All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem. ... there are some obscure cases where a query against a WAL-mode database can return SQLITE_BUSY.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0084:27,93 (UNVERIFIED, R-SQLITE): WAL gives readers-don't-block-writers but SQLite still serialises writers, so one writer connection or a queued write path, never a pool; read via search, not first-party.
best_practice.source_says: First-party sqlite.org confirms: one writer at a time under WAL, readers and the writer run concurrently, and multi-process use is fine only on one host with no network filesystem.
best_practice.note: [documented] FIRST first-party verification of the R-SQLITE item; the rule stands unchanged. Two additions for the store design: (1) a repo whose git common dir sits on a network share breaks WAL, so doctor should check the mount; (2) readers can also see SQLITE_BUSY in 'obscure cases', so busy_timeout belongs on reader connections too, not only the writer.

best_practice.source_quote: rusqlite 0.40.2 (2026-08-08). busy_timeout: Set a busy handler that sleeps for a specified amount of time when a table is locked ... New connections default to a 5000ms timeout. Connection: Send, !Sync.
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0084:27,63 / arch-design 9.2: rusqlite 0.40.2, bundled, open with journal_mode=WAL and a busy_timeout, one writer connection, reader connections may be plural.
best_practice.source_says: Version still current; busy_timeout exists and rusqlite already applies a 5000 ms default on open; Connection is Send but not Sync.
best_practice.note: [documented] crates.io confirms 0.40.2 is max_version. Consequence for the adapter: !Sync means 'one writer connection' must be owned by one thread or behind a Mutex/channel (the ADR's 'queued write path'), and plural readers must be one-per-thread. Keep the explicit busy_timeout call so the value is a recorded decision rather than rusqlite's default.

best_practice.source_quote: M-LATEST-EDITION: When creating a new crate or workspace, set edition to the latest stable edition (at least 2024 at the time of writing); the resolver field is generally not needed. Rust 1.85.0 (2025-02-20): We are excited to announce that the Rust 2024 Edition is now stable!

best_practice.note: [documented] blog.rust-lang.org/2025/02/20/Rust-1.85.0/ for the edition; MS guideline page generated 2026-08-19.

best_practice.source_quote: "3" (edition = "2024" default, requires Rust 1.84+): Change the default for resolver.incompatible-rust-versions from allow to fallback. With the fallback setting, the resolver will prefer packages with a Rust version that is less than or equal to your own Rust version. rust-version: cargo add will auto-select the dependency's version requirement to be the latest version compatible with your rust-v
best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0083:49 / arch-design 9.3: rust-toolchain.toml pins an exact rustc; package.rust-version is not used as a substitute (a pin and a floor answer different questions).
best_practice.source_says: Cargo treats them as complementary, not alternatives: edition 2024's resolver 3 switches on the MSRV-aware resolver, which only does anything when package.rust-version is set. Microsoft M-MSRV: an MSRV should be set when crates are first created.
best_practice.note: [documented] The pin is correct for a binary you control, but omitting rust-version leaves the edition-2024 MSRV-aware resolver and cargo add's version selection inert. Consider setting workspace.package.rust-version equal to the pinned channel so both mechanisms agree; the ADR's rejection was aimed at substitution, not co-existence. Also read: cargo/reference/rust-version.html, config.html.

best_practice.source_quote: The workspace.lints table is where you define lint configuration to be inherited by members of a workspace ... [workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid" ... [lints] workspace = true. best_practice.corpus_says: ADR-0083:53 / arch-design 9.3: [workspace.lints.rust] and [workspace.lints.clippy] in the root manifest; every member carries [lints] workspace = true.

Microsoft M-STATIC-VERIFICATION: pedantic = { level = "warn", priority = -1 } ... # nursery ... optional. M-

best_practice.note: [documented] The corpus is careful that reading the environment once at the edge is not unsafe; the guide agrees. Also consistent with Microsoft M-MOCKABLE-SYSCALLS (environment-dependent inputs should be injectable).

rows.source_quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed concurrently ... Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time. However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

rows.source_quote: The short answer is: yes. And the main reason is to make updates intentional and avoid surprises. ... I would recommend to pin the Rust toolchain to a specific version using a rust-toolchain.toml file
rows.corpus_says: Pin vs floor answer different questions; 'the "pin for a binary you control" framing is the blog's' (swatinem.de), corroborated by RFC 3537
rows.source_says: The swatinem post (2025-02-15) never mentions package.rust-version, MSRV floors, libraries or binaries; it argues for pinning to make updates intentional. The application framing is RFC 3537's: 'controlling their MSRV via rust-toolchain.toml ... (e.g. an application with a vetted toolchain)'.
rows.note: [documented] The conclusion (pin the toolchain for this project shape) stands, but ADR-0083:118 attributes the 'pin for a binary you control' framing to the wrong source: it is the RFC's (https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3537-msrv-resolver.html), and the blog contributes only the general 'pin, and make updates intentional' argument.
rows.second_note: [documented] Drift holds and is doubly grounded: the corpus never read the blog (evidence-augmentation:401 'URL not returned'), so ADR-0083:118's attribution was made without the source, and the source, now read, lacks it. The blog gives only 'pin, and make updates intentional' (it does support ADR-0083:29's clippy-bump worry: 'new lints every 6 weeks ... causing friction'). Cite RFC 3537 alone.
rows.claim_text: A pin and a floor answer different questions and are not substitutes; the product is one binary plus internal crates, so the pin is the mechanism [documented, [blog] swatinem.de + [1P] RFC 3537 — the "pin for a binary you control" framing is the blog's]
